## Today

::: {.objectives}
1. **Use vs availability** — the central idea of habitat selection
2. Johnson's **four orders** of selection
3. The RSF: what it is, and what the coefficients mean
4. **Availability is a decision**, and it drives your conclusions
5. Fitting, weighting, and the multiple-animal problem
:::

# 1 · The central idea {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## Selection is a comparison

An animal **selects** a resource when it uses it **disproportionately to its
availability**.

::: {.incremental}
- Use alone tells you nothing. A wolf in a landscape that is 95% forest will
  be found mostly in forest whether or not it prefers forest
- So every selection analysis needs two samples:
  - **Used** — where the animal was
  - **Available** — where it could have been
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
The second sample is not data. **You construct it**, and the construction
encodes a hypothesis. Most disagreements about habitat selection results are
disagreements about availability.
:::

---

## Johnson's four orders (1980)
| Order | Question | Available = |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **1st** | Where is the species' range? | The planet |
| **2nd** | Where does this individual put its home range? | The study area / population range |
| **3rd** | Where within its home range does it go? | The home range |
| **4th** | Which items does it take at a site? | Items at the site |

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
The **same animal** can show opposite results at different orders. A deer may
place its home range in forest (2nd order) yet prefer clearings within it
(3rd order). Always state your order — it is the definition of "available".
:::

---

## The RSF

$$w(\mathbf{x}) = \exp(\beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k)$$

$w(\mathbf{x})$ is the **relative** probability of use, proportional to the
true probability by an unknown constant.

::: {.incremental}
- Fitted with logistic regression on used (1) vs available (0) points
- There is **no intercept you can interpret** — it absorbs the arbitrary
  number of available points you drew
- Only **relative** statements are licensed: "twice as likely as", never
  "40% probability of use"
:::

---

## Used–available is not case–control

::: {.incremental}
- "Available" points are not known **absences**. The animal may well have used
  them; you just did not observe it
- Formally, the used–available design fits an **inhomogeneous Poisson point
  process**, and logistic regression is a computational device for it
- This is why the **infinitely weighted logistic regression** trick works:
  give available points a huge weight and the logistic coefficients converge
  to the correct point-process coefficients
:::

. . .

```r
d$w <- ifelse(d$case_, 1, 5000)
glm(case_ ~ elevation + grassland, data = d,
    family = binomial(), weights = d$w)
```

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
Your RSF gives $\hat\beta = 0.69$ for a standardised NDVI covariate. What can
you correctly say?

- [ ] There is a 69% probability the animal uses high-NDVI areas
- [x] A one-SD increase in NDVI roughly **doubles** the relative probability of use
- [ ] NDVI explains 69% of the variation in use
- [ ] The animal uses high-NDVI areas 69% of the time

::: {.quiz-feedback}
RSF coefficients are on the log scale, so the effect is multiplicative:
$e^{0.69} \approx 2$. A one-standard-deviation increase in NDVI **doubles the
relative probability of use**, holding the other covariates fixed.

"Relative" is doing essential work in that sentence. The RSF is proportional
to the probability of use by an unknown constant — the intercept depends
entirely on how many available points you happened to draw — so absolute
probabilities are not available to you.

Standardising covariates before fitting is what makes "one SD" meaningful and
lets you compare effect sizes across covariates measured in different units.
:::
:::

# 2 · Availability, the hard part {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## Three decisions

::: {.incremental}
1. **The domain.** Study area? MCP? KDE? Buffer around the track? This *is*
   your choice of Johnson order.
2. **How many points.** Too few and the estimates are noisy; the coefficients
   should **stabilise** as you add more. Check that they do.
3. **How they are distributed.** Uniform random is the default. But should
   inaccessible areas (open water, cliffs, the other side of a motorway) be
   "available" at all?
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
Changing the availability domain can reverse the sign of a coefficient. This
is not a flaw in the method — it is the method working. Different domains ask
different questions.
:::

---

## How many available points?

::: {.incremental}
- There is no magic number. The practical test: **increase the number until
  the coefficients stop changing**
- Typically thousands to tens of thousands per animal
- With infinite weighting, more available points is always better — the only
  cost is computation
:::

. . .

```r
for (n in c(1e3, 5e3, 2e4, 1e5)) {
  d <- random_points(trk, n = n) |> extract_covariates(covs)
  # ... refit, record coefficients, plot them against n
}
```

---

## The functional response

Selection is not a fixed property of an animal.

::: {.incremental}
- An animal in a forest-rich landscape may show **weak** selection for forest;
  the same animal in a forest-poor landscape shows **strong** selection
- So $\beta$ depends on availability — the *functional response in habitat
  use* (Mysterud & Ims 1998)
- Pooling individuals across different landscapes without modelling this
  averages away the very thing you are studying
:::

. . .

Practical consequence: report the availability each individual faced, and
consider modelling $\beta$ as a function of it.

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
Two studies of the same wolf population reach opposite conclusions about
selection for roads. Study A used available points drawn from the whole
national park; study B drew them from within each wolf's home range. Who is
right?

- [ ] Study A — a larger availability domain is more objective
- [ ] Study B — home ranges are the only biologically meaningful domain
- [x] Both, and they answer different questions
- [ ] Neither; the analysis is invalid without known absences

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Study A asks a **second-order** question: given the whole park, do wolves put
their home ranges in areas with more or fewer roads? Study B asks a
**third-order** question: within the home range a wolf has already chosen,
does it approach or avoid roads?

These routinely give opposite answers, and the pattern is common and
interpretable: wolves may settle in road-poor parts of the park (avoidance at
2nd order) while using road verges and tracks as travel routes once there
(selection at 3rd order).

Neither study is wrong. Both are incomplete if they do not **state the order**
and the availability domain — which is why that belongs in the abstract, not
buried in the methods.
:::
:::

# 3 · Fitting it properly {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## The workflow in `amt`

```r
library(amt)

rsf_data <- trk |>
  filter(id == "Cilla") |>
  random_points(n = nrow(trk) * 20) |>     # available within the MCP
  extract_covariates(covs) |>
  mutate(w = ifelse(case_, 1, 5000))

fit <- glm(case_ ~ elevation + slope + grassland + trees,
           data = rsf_data, family = binomial(), weights = w)
```

. . .

`random_points()` on a track defaults to the MCP of that track — a third-order
analysis. Pass an `hr` object to control the domain explicitly.

---

## Standardise your covariates

```r
rsf_data <- rsf_data |>
  mutate(across(c(elevation, slope, grassland, trees),
                \(z) as.numeric(scale(z))))
```

::: {.incremental}
- Makes coefficients **comparable** across covariates with different units
- "Per one standard deviation" is an interpretable effect size
- Improves numerical conditioning
- **Keep the means and SDs** — you need them to back-transform for prediction
:::

---

## More than one animal

The wrong way: pool all fixes and fit one model. Individuals differ, and the
animal with most fixes dominates.

::: {.incremental}
- **Two-stage**: fit each animal separately, then summarise the coefficients
  across individuals (mean, SE, a t-test against zero). Transparent, robust,
  easy to explain
- **Mixed models**: random intercept **and random slopes** per individual. Muff
  et al. (2020) show the random slopes are essential — without them you
  under-estimate the uncertainty badly
- A random intercept alone is *not* enough
:::

. . .

For 6 buffalo, the two-stage approach is honest and adequate. For 60, use a
mixed model.

---

## Validation

$R^2$ is not available for a point-process model. Use instead:

::: {.incremental}
- **k-fold cross-validation with used–available data** (Boyce et al. 2002):
  bin the predicted RSF values, and check that the number of *withheld* used
  points per bin increases with the bin's rank. Report the Spearman
  correlation
- **Withhold whole individuals**, not random points — otherwise
  autocorrelation leaks the answer into your test set
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
A model can have highly significant coefficients and no predictive ability at
all. With tens of thousands of points, *everything* is significant. Report
effect sizes and validation, not p-values.
:::

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
You fit an RSF with 25,000 available points per animal and every covariate has
p < 0.001. What should you conclude?

- [ ] All the covariates matter a lot
- [x] Almost nothing — p-values are driven by the number of available points, which you chose
- [ ] The model is overfitted
- [ ] You should reduce the number of available points to get honest p-values

::: {.quiz-feedback}
You chose the sample size, so you chose the p-values. Doubling the available
points roughly halves the standard errors without adding any information about
the animal. In used–available designs, p-values are close to meaningless.

What *is* informative: the **effect sizes** ($e^\beta$, on standardised
covariates), their **confidence intervals**, the **consistency across
individuals**, and **out-of-sample validation**.

And no — reducing the available sample to manufacture plausible p-values would
be worse. It throws away precision in the estimate of availability to make a
statistic look respectable. Report effect sizes.
:::
:::

:::

---

## Recap

::: {.incremental}
- Selection = use **relative to availability**. You construct availability
- State your **Johnson order** — it is the definition of available
- RSF coefficients are **log relative** effects: $e^\beta$, and no intercept
- Availability domain, sample size and distribution all change the answer
- Individuals differ: two-stage, or mixed models **with random slopes**
- p-values are meaningless here. Effect sizes and validation are not
:::
